Final-year project · explained from zero
SONA

Self-supervised Online Neural Audio engine

How a small neural network removes background noise from speech, explained one idea at a time.

You do not need to know anything about audio, maths or machine learning to read this. Every term is explained the first time it appears, every number from the project is shown with what it means, and four hands-on demos plus a listening lab let you hear and see the ideas for yourself.

Part A

Sound from scratch

Before we can remove noise, we need to know what sound actually is and how a computer holds it.

Chapter 1

The problem SONA solves

In one sentenceRecordings of people talking almost always contain unwanted sound, and SONA's job is to turn that unwanted sound down while leaving the voice untouched.

Think of a phone call made next to a busy road, a video meeting with a fan running, or a voice note recorded in a cafe. In every case the microphone does not know which sounds you care about. It captures everything: the voice and the traffic, the voice and the fan, the voice and other people talking. All of it arrives mixed together.

That mix causes real problems:

  • Listeners get tired. Your brain works hard to separate speech from noise, so noisy calls are exhausting even when you can follow them.
  • Words get lost. When the noise is loud enough, short sounds like "s", "t" and "f" disappear completely, and meaning goes with them.
  • Machines struggle too. Voice assistants and automatic captioning make more mistakes on noisy audio.
  • Hearing aids amplify everything. A hearing aid that makes the voice louder also makes the noise louder, unless something separates them first.

The goal of this project, called SONA, is a system that takes noisy speech in and gives cleaner speech out, quickly enough to work live and small enough to run on a cheap, low-power computer.

Everyday comparison: imagine a photo of a friend taken through a dirty window. You want to wipe the dirt off the photo without smudging your friend's face. Noise removal is the audio version: wipe off the noise, keep the voice sharp.

What the name SONA means

SONA stands for Self-supervised Online Neural Audio engine. Each word describes part of the original plan for the project:

S

Self-supervised

Normally a model learns from a teacher: for every noisy clip we hand it the clean answer. "Self-supervised" means the system can judge and improve its own output without being given the clean answer. SONA does this with a separate quality-estimating model (TorchAudio-SQUIM) that scores how good speech sounds from the audio alone, acting as its own teacher.

O

Online

"Online" here does not mean "on the internet". It means while running: adjusting itself on each new recording as it arrives, after it has been deployed, instead of only learning once beforehand. Everything still runs on your own machine.

N

Neural

The decisions are made by a neural network (Part D), not by fixed formulas. That is what lets SONA recognise what speech looks like.

A

Audio engine

It works on sound, and it is an "engine": a core that other things are built around, such as the controller, the app and, in Phase 2, the hardware device.

Put together, the name describes the project's founding idea: a neural audio engine that keeps improving itself on each new recording, live, without ever needing the clean version.

Everyday comparison: a musician who tunes their guitar by ear before every song. Nobody hands them the "correct" notes; they listen to themselves and adjust. That is the self-supervised, online part.

How the finished project relates to the name. The project tested this self-adjusting idea carefully (Chapter 26). It turned out to give almost no extra benefit: without safety limits it even made results worse, and with them the gain was about zero. So the system you see working today relies mainly on the N and A: a well-trained neural network whose settings are fixed after training. The self-supervised online part is still in the app as an experimental switch, and the name stayed with the project. Reporting that honestly is part of the research.

Why it matters for SONA: the whole project is judged on one question: after SONA has processed a recording, is the speech cleaner and still easy to understand? Every chapter that follows serves that question.
Chapter 2

What sound is

In one sentenceSound is a tiny, very fast back-and-forth wobble in air pressure, and two properties of that wobble, how fast it repeats and how big it is, are what we hear as pitch and loudness.

When someone speaks, their vocal cords vibrate. That vibration pushes on the air, making the air pressure rise and fall slightly, very quickly. These pressure ripples travel outward, reach your ear, and push your eardrum in and out. Your brain turns that motion into what you hear.

Two properties of these ripples matter most:

Frequency → pitch

How many times per second the pressure goes up and down. It is measured in hertz (Hz): 100 Hz means 100 cycles per second. A low male voice vibrates around 100 Hz, a high female voice around 250 Hz, and the hiss of an "s" sound reaches 4,000 to 8,000 Hz. People can hear roughly 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.

Amplitude → loudness

How big the pressure swings are. A whisper makes tiny swings; a shout makes large ones. Because our ears handle an enormous range, loudness is usually measured in decibels, which Chapter 4 explains.

Real sounds are never a single clean pitch. A voice is a mixture of many frequencies at once: a basic pitch (the fundamental) plus many higher harmonics, and the shape of your mouth makes some of them stronger than others. That pattern of strong and weak frequencies is what makes an "ah" sound different from an "ee". Noise is also a mixture of frequencies, usually a messier one.

Everyday comparison: drop a stone in a pond and ripples spread out. Small stones make small ripples (quiet), big stones make big ones (loud). Ripples packed close together are high pitch; ripples spread far apart are low pitch.
Why it matters for SONA: speech energy mostly sits between about 100 Hz and 8,000 Hz. That fact decides how SONA records audio (next chapter) and where it looks for the voice.
Chapter 3

How a computer stores sound

In one sentenceA computer stores sound as a long list of numbers, each one measuring the air pressure at one instant, taken thousands of times per second.

A microphone turns pressure into an electrical signal. A chip called an analogue-to-digital converter then measures that signal at regular, very short intervals and writes down a number each time. This is called sampling. The list of numbers that results is the waveform.

  • Sample rate is how many measurements are taken per second. SONA uses 16,000 samples per second (16 kHz). So one second of audio is a list of 16,000 numbers, and an 8-second clip is 128,000 numbers.
  • The highest pitch you can capture is half the sample rate. This rule is called the Nyquist limit. At 16 kHz the limit is 8,000 Hz, which covers almost all of the information in speech. That is why speech systems commonly use 16 kHz: higher rates add data without adding much to intelligibility.
  • Each number is a level between −1 and +1. 0 is silence (normal air pressure), and +1 or −1 is the loudest the system can store. Going past that causes clipping, which sounds harsh and distorted.
Everyday comparison: a film is a series of still photos shown quickly enough that you see motion. Digital audio is a series of pressure measurements taken quickly enough that you hear continuous sound. 16,000 "photos" per second is plenty for speech.

The key difficulty is visible right here: when a voice and a fan are both present, each number in the list is simply voice + fan added together. The list does not label which part came from where. Separating them is the whole challenge.

Why it matters for SONA: every model in this project receives exactly this, a list of 16,000 numbers per second, and must output another list of the same length with the noise turned down.
Chapter 4

Decibels and signal-to-noise ratio

In one sentenceDecibels measure loudness as a ratio on a stretched scale, and the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) says how much louder the voice is than the noise.

Our hearing covers an enormous range: the loudest sound you can bear is about a million million times more powerful than the quietest you can detect. Writing such numbers directly is impractical, so engineers use a logarithmic scale called the decibel (dB). The rules of thumb:

Change in dBPower becomesAmplitude becomesWhat you hear
+3 dB2×1.4×a just-noticeable increase
+6 dB4×2×clearly louder
+10 dB10×3.2×sounds roughly twice as loud
+20 dB100×10×a big jump
−10 dB÷10÷3.2sounds roughly half as loud

A decibel value is always a comparison against something. When we compare the voice against the noise, we get the signal-to-noise ratio:

SNR (dB) = 10 × log10( power of the voice ÷ power of the noise )
  • +10 dB: the voice is 10 times more powerful than the noise. Easy to follow.
  • 0 dB: voice and noise are equally powerful. Tiring, but usually understandable.
  • −5 dB: the noise is about 3 times more powerful than the voice. Very hard.

The library clips in the SONA app are labelled this way: "+5 dB" (cafe babble), "0 dB" (vacuum cleaner) and "−5 dB" (copy machine, the hardest).

Why it matters for SONA: almost every score in this project is in decibels. When you later read "+9.9 dB improvement", it means the cleaned speech is closer to the clean original by the same kind of ratio you just heard change with the slider.
Chapter 5

Why noise removal is hard

In one sentenceVoice and noise overlap in time and in pitch, and much real noise changes constantly or even sounds like speech, so no simple rule can pull them apart.

If noise always lived at different pitches from the voice, removing it would be easy: block those pitches. Real life is not that kind.

Overlap in pitch

A vacuum cleaner or air conditioner spreads energy across almost every frequency, including the ones speech uses. Blocking those frequencies would block the voice too.

Overlap in time

The noise is present while the person is speaking, not only in the gaps. We cannot simply mute the noisy moments.

Noise that changes

A steady hum is stationary: it stays the same, so it can be measured once and subtracted. Traffic, door slams and typing are non-stationary: they come and go unpredictably.

Noise that is speech

"Babble" is other people talking. It has the same pitches and rhythm as the voice you want. Telling the target voice from background voices needs understanding of patterns, not a fixed rule.

Why it matters for SONA: this is exactly why the project moves from fixed rules (classical methods) to a model that learns what speech looks like. The results later show the learned model beats every fixed rule by a wide margin, and also show which noises are still hardest (babble and short clicks).
Part B

Seeing sound

A list of numbers is hard to reason about. These chapters turn it into a picture where voice and noise look different.

Chapter 6

Frequencies and the Fourier transform

In one sentenceAny sound can be described as a set of pure tones added together, and the Fourier transform is the maths that works out which tones, and how strong each one is.

In the 1800s, the mathematician Joseph Fourier showed that any repeating shape can be built by adding up simple waves (sine waves) of different frequencies and strengths. Run that in reverse and you can take any sound and find its ingredient list: "this much at 140 Hz, this much at 280 Hz, a little at 3,000 Hz…". That ingredient list is called the spectrum. The method for computing it is the Fourier transform, and the fast computer version is called the FFT (Fast Fourier Transform).

Everyday comparison: a smoothie tastes like one thing, but it was made from separate fruits. The Fourier transform is like a machine that tastes the smoothie and tells you "40% banana, 30% strawberry, 30% mango". It recovers the ingredients from the mixture.
Demo 2 · Build a sound from pure tones

Mix three pure tones and watch the waveform and the spectrum

Top: the waveform (the list of numbers over time). Bottom: the spectrum (how much of each frequency is present). Notice how a complicated wobbly waveform is just three simple ingredients.

Why it matters for SONA: in a spectrum, voice and noise often look different even when they are mixed together in the waveform. A voice shows as a neat comb of harmonics; a fan shows as a smooth spread. That difference is what SONA learns to spot.
Chapter 7

Spectrograms: a picture of sound over time

In one sentenceWe chop the sound into many tiny pieces, find the pitch ingredients of each piece, draw each piece as one thin column of colour, and line the columns up from left to right.

Step 1 · Why one spectrum is not enough

Chapter 6 showed how to find the ingredients (the pitches) of a sound. But that gives one answer for the whole sound at once.

Now think about saying the word "sun". It starts with "s", a hissing sound made of high pitches. Then comes "u", a vowel made of low, steady pitches. Then "n", a soft humming sound. If you find the ingredients of the whole word at once, you get all three mixed into one answer, and you can no longer tell which sound happened when.

Speech changes every few hundredths of a second, so we need the ingredients moment by moment, not once for the whole recording.

Everyday comparison: one photo of a running dog taken with a very long exposure is just a blur. A video is many short photos in a row, so you can see every step. A single spectrum is the blurry photo; a spectrogram is the video.

Step 2 · The recipe, in plain words

  1. Cut out a tiny piece. Take the first 512 numbers of the recording. At 16,000 numbers per second, that piece is only 32 thousandths of a second long (an eye blink takes about 100 to 150 thousandths). The piece is so short that the sound barely changes inside it.
  2. Find that piece's ingredients. Run the Fourier transform from Chapter 6 on just this piece. The answer is a list of 257 strengths: how much of the lowest pitch is present, how much of the next pitch up, and so on, all the way to the highest pitch (8,000 Hz).
  3. Turn that list into one column of colour. Draw the 257 strengths as a thin vertical strip of little boxes. The bottom box is the lowest pitch, the top box is the highest. A strong pitch is drawn bright (yellow or orange); a weak one is drawn dark (purple or black).
  4. Move forward a tiny bit and repeat. Slide along by 128 numbers (8 thousandths of a second) and do the same again. Because each step is shorter than the piece, neighbouring pieces overlap: each new piece shares three quarters of its sound with the previous one, so nothing is ever missed at the joins.
  5. Put the columns side by side. One column every 8 thousandths of a second means 125 columns for every second of sound. Lined up left to right, they form the spectrogram.
Demo 3 · Build a spectrogram yourself

Drag the slider (or press Play) to move the piece along the sound

The test sound has three parts: a whistle that rises in pitch, then a voice-like hum, then a burst of hiss. Watch the orange box on the waveform (the piece being looked at), its ingredients on the right, and the spectrogram growing one column at a time below. Step 3 · How to read a spectrogram

Left to right = time

The left edge is the start of the recording, the right edge the end. Each thin column is one 32-thousandths-of-a-second piece.

Bottom to top = pitch

Low pitches (deep voices, hums) are near the bottom; high pitches (hiss, "s" sounds) are near the top. The top edge is 8,000 Hz.

Colour = strength

Bright yellow and orange mean a pitch is loud at that moment. Dark purple and black mean it is quiet or absent.

With practice, different sounds have recognisable shapes, exactly like in the demo:

  • A voice makes several parallel bright stripes stacked above each other: the basic pitch at the bottom and its harmonics above it. The stripes start and stop as syllables come and go.
  • A whistle or a single tone makes one thin line, which slopes up when the pitch rises.
  • Hiss and fan noise make a grainy colour spread across many pitches, with no neat stripes.
  • Silence is dark.

This is the key to the whole project: in the waveform, voice and noise are mixed into one wobbly line, but in the spectrogram they often look different (neat stripes versus grainy spread), even when they happen at the same moment. That difference is what SONA learns to spot. In Chapter 22 you will see real spectrograms of a voice with a vacuum cleaner, before and after SONA: the grainy noise fades and the voice stripes remain.

Step 4 · Why pieces of 32 thousandths of a second?

It is a balance between two kinds of detail, a bit like choosing a camera's shutter speed:

Longer pieces

See pitch very precisely (good for telling close notes apart) but blur quick changes together, like a slow shutter blurs a moving car.

Shorter pieces

Catch quick changes sharply (the start of a "t" or a door slam) but see pitch only roughly.

For speech recorded at 16,000 numbers per second, pieces of 32 thousandths of a second, moved along 8 thousandths at a time, are the standard compromise used across speech research.

For the curious: the technical names

Engineers call the whole process the Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT). Each piece is a frame (512 samples). The step between pieces is the hop (128 samples), so neighbouring frames overlap by 75%. Before the Fourier transform, each frame is multiplied by a smooth bell-shaped curve called a Hann window, which fades the piece in and out so that the sudden cut at its edges does not create fake high pitches. Each of the 257 strengths is a frequency bin, 31.25 Hz wide (16,000 ÷ 512). Turning a spectrogram back into sound is the inverse STFT with overlap-add (Chapter 10).

Why it matters for SONA: SONA never works on the raw list of numbers directly. It works on this picture, decides how much of each part to keep, and turns the edited picture back into sound.
Chapter 8

Bands and features: summarising the picture

In one sentenceSONA groups the 257 frequencies into 32 bands spaced the way human hearing works, and describes each band in each frame with three numbers.

Our ears are very precise at low pitches and much less precise at high ones. We can tell 100 Hz from 120 Hz easily, but 6,000 Hz and 6,020 Hz sound the same. The Bark scale captures this: it divides frequency into bands that are narrow at the bottom and wide at the top, matching how hearing resolves pitch.

SONA groups the 257 bins into 32 Bark bands. This has two benefits: the model makes 32 decisions per frame instead of 257, which keeps it small, and each decision lines up with how a person would perceive the change.

For each band in each 8 ms frame, SONA calculates three features (numbers that describe what is going on):

1 · Log band energy

How loud this band is right now, on a decibel-like scale. Speech bands light up when someone talks.

2 · Temporal delta

How much that loudness changed since the previous frame. Speech starts and stops quickly; a fan stays steady.

3 · Spectral flux

How much new energy just appeared. It spikes at the start of syllables and at sudden noises.

So the model's input is a grid: 3 features × 32 bands × however many frames the clip has. An 8-second clip has about 1,000 frames.

Why it matters for SONA: these features are deliberately simple. The project's claim is that a small network reading simple features in context can beat hand-tuned rules, and that it can do so cheaply enough for small hardware.
Chapter 9

Magnitude and phase

In one sentenceEach frequency in each frame has a strength (magnitude) and a timing offset (phase); SONA's main model edits the strength and keeps the original timing.

The FFT gives two numbers for every frequency bin. The magnitude says how strong that frequency is. The phase says where in its cycle the wave was when the frame started, a kind of timing information. You need both to turn a spectrogram back into exact sound.

Our ears are much more sensitive to magnitude than to phase. So the simplest and most common approach, used by SONA's main model, is: change the magnitudes, keep the noisy phase. It works well, but the phase still carries a little of the noise. Chapter 25 describes a variant (the "complex mask") that corrects phase as well, and what it gained and lost.

Everyday comparison: a group of people clapping. Magnitude is how hard each person claps; phase is exactly when each person claps. Changing how hard some people clap changes the sound a lot; nudging their timing by a hair changes it much less.
Part C

Removing noise

Now that sound is a picture, removing noise becomes deciding how much of each part of the picture to keep.

Chapter 10

The core idea: a mask

In one sentenceFor every band in every frame, SONA picks a number between 0 and 1 that says how much to keep, multiplies the spectrogram by these numbers, and turns the result back into sound.

This grid of keep-amounts is called a mask (or gain mask). A value of 1 means "this is voice, keep all of it". A value of 0 means "this is noise, remove it". Values in between turn the band down partly, which matters when voice and noise share a band.

Turning the picture back into sound is the inverse STFT: each edited frame is converted back to a short piece of waveform, and the overlapping pieces are added together (overlap-add). Because the Hann window and the 75% overlap fit together perfectly, an untouched spectrogram turns back into exactly the original sound. The project's tests check this.

Everyday comparison: a sound engineer's mixing desk has a volume fader for every channel. A mask is like having a separate fader for each of 32 pitch ranges, and moving all of them 125 times per second, automatically.
Why it matters for SONA: because every method outputs the same kind of mask, the only real question becomes "who predicts the best mask?". That is what makes the comparison in this project fair.
Chapter 11

Classical methods, and why they fail on real noise

In one sentenceClassical methods guess the noise level, then compute the mask from a fixed formula, which works for steady hums and breaks on changing, speech-like noise.

Before machine learning, noise reduction relied on digital signal processing (DSP) formulas. All four classical methods in SONA follow the same two steps:

  1. Estimate the noise. SONA uses minimum statistics: in each band, look back over recent frames and take the quietest level seen. The idea is that speech has pauses, so the quietest moments reveal the noise floor.
  2. Compute the mask from a formula comparing each band's current level to that noise estimate.

Spectral subtraction

Subtract the estimated noise power from each band (Boll, 1979). Simple, but over-subtracting leaves a "musical noise" of random beeps, and under-subtracting leaves noise behind.

Wiener filter

Keep each band in proportion to how much stronger it is than the noise: mask = SNR ÷ (1 + SNR). It estimates SNR with a smoothed "decision-directed" rule (Ephraim and Malah, 1984). The strongest classical method in theory.

Hard threshold

If a band is above a threshold over the noise, keep it fully; otherwise remove it completely. All-or-nothing.

Soft threshold

Like the hard threshold, but shrink bands gradually instead of switching them off (Donoho, 1995).

They share four weaknesses: the noise estimate assumes the noise is steady; the decision uses loudness only, with no idea of what speech looks like; quiet parts of speech (soft consonants) look like noise and get removed; and the settings are tuned by hand. Try it yourself:

Demo 4 · Try to clean a spectrogram with a simple rule

Raise the threshold to remove more noise, and watch how much speech you lose

A toy spectrogram: bright stripes are speech (some loud vowels, some quiet consonants), the grainy background is noise. The rule is a classical hard threshold: keep a cell only if it is louder than the threshold.

Noise removed—
Speech kept—
Verdict—

No threshold gets both numbers to 100%, because some quiet speech is weaker than some noise. A fixed rule cannot tell them apart; only knowledge of what speech looks like over time can. On the real VoiceBank test, every classical method ended up making the speech worse than doing nothing (Chapter 23).

Chapter 12

One front-end, many brains: a fair comparison

In one sentenceEvery method in SONA shares the same input processing, the same kind of output and the same scoring code, so the only thing being compared is how each one decides the mask.

Research comparisons are often unfair by accident: method A uses a different spectrogram, a different sample rate or a different scoring script from method B, so you cannot tell whether A won because of its idea or because of those differences. SONA removes that doubt.

Everyday comparison: testing cooks fairly means giving them the same ingredients, the same kitchen and the same judges. Then the difference in the food comes from the cook alone.
Why it matters for SONA: this design is one of the project's main contributions, and it is why the conference paper can say the learned model, not some side detail, is responsible for the improvement.
Part D

Neural networks from scratch

The classical rules failed because they cannot recognise speech. A neural network can learn to. These chapters explain how, with no maths background needed.

Chapter 13

What a neural network is

In one sentenceA neural network is a large formula with hundreds of thousands of adjustable numbers (weights), arranged in layers, that turns an input into an output.

The basic unit is an artificial neuron. It takes some input numbers, multiplies each by a weight (how important that input is), adds them up, and passes the total through a small bending function called an activation. The bend matters: without it, stacking neurons would only ever produce a straight-line formula, which cannot capture complicated patterns.

output = activation( w1 × input1 + w2 × input2 + … + bias )

Neurons are arranged in layers. The first layer reads the input features; each later layer reads the previous layer's outputs and builds slightly more abstract patterns ("energy rising in these bands" → "this looks like the start of a vowel"). The final layer outputs the answer, which for SONA is the mask.

All the weights together are the network's parameters. SONA's main model has 722,209 of them, stored in a 2.8 MB file. That sounds like a lot, but modern image or language models have millions to billions; SONA is deliberately tiny so it can run on small hardware.

Everyday comparison: imagine a huge mixing desk with 722,209 knobs. Each knob changes how much one small signal affects another. Set randomly, the desk produces nonsense. Set correctly, it turns noisy audio into a good mask. Training is the process of finding the right knob positions.
Chapter 14

How a network learns

In one sentenceWe show the network thousands of noisy clips whose clean versions we know, measure how wrong its output is, and nudge every weight slightly in the direction that makes it less wrong, over and over.

  1. Training pairs. Each example is a noisy clip plus the clean clip it was made from. The clean one is the "answer key".
  2. Forward pass. The network predicts a mask for the noisy clip; the mask is applied; out comes its attempt at clean speech.
  3. Loss. A loss function scores how far that attempt is from the true clean clip. Lower is better. (Chapter 17 explains SONA's loss.)
  4. Backpropagation. Calculus works out, for every one of the 722,209 weights, which direction of change would reduce the loss. This set of directions is the gradient.
  5. Update. Every weight moves a tiny step in its helpful direction. The step size is the learning rate (SONA uses 0.0003). An optimiser called AdamW adapts the step for each weight automatically.
  6. Repeat. SONA processes clips in batches of 8. 2,000 training clips ÷ 8 = 250 updates per full pass (an epoch). Training ran 50 epochs, about 12,500 updates, on a free Kaggle NVIDIA T4 graphics card.
Everyday comparison: learning to throw darts blindfolded while a friend tells you how far from the bullseye each dart landed. You adjust your arm a little after each throw. After thousands of throws you are consistently close, even though nobody ever told you the exact arm movement.

Training, validation and test data

If you study only the exact questions that will be on an exam, you can score well without understanding anything. Networks can do the same: memorise the training clips instead of learning speech in general. This is called overfitting. The defence is to keep separate data:

  • Training data is what the network learns from.
  • Validation data is checked during development to choose settings.
  • Test data is held back and used only for the final score. SONA's main test set, VoiceBank-DEMAND test, uses speakers and noise types the model never heard in training. A second test set, MS-SNSD, comes from an entirely different collection.

Two more tricks fight overfitting: SONA trains on random 2-second crops of each clip, so it sees slightly different pieces each time, and uses dropout (randomly ignoring 10% of signals during training) so no single connection becomes too important.

Chapter 15

The building blocks inside SONA's model

In one sentenceSONA's model combines convolutions (pattern detectors that slide over the spectrogram), gates (switches that decide what passes), and a recurrent layer (memory over time).

Convolution

A small grid of weights, here 3 frames × 3 bands, slides across the feature picture. At each position it multiplies and adds, producing a strong output where its pattern appears. Different filters learn different patterns: onsets, steady hums, harmonic stacks. One set of weights is reused everywhere, which keeps the model small.

Dilation

A dilated convolution skips frames: dilation 2 looks at frames t, t−2, t−4; dilation 8 looks at t, t−8, t−16. Stacking dilations 1, 2, 4 and 8 lets four small filters see about 31 frames, roughly a quarter of a second, of history.

Causal

The filters only look backwards in time, never at future frames. That is essential for live use: a live device cannot know what someone will say next.

Gating

Each block produces two outputs: a candidate signal and a "gate" between 0 and 1 (from a sigmoid function). The result is candidate × gate, so the block can switch each feature on only where it helps.

Residual connection

Each block adds its output to its input instead of replacing it. Information can flow straight through, which makes deep stacks train reliably.

Normalisation

Rescales the numbers inside the network to a standard range, so training is stable. (SONA's version looks across the whole clip; Phase 2 replaces it with a per-frame version for live use.)

GRU (memory)

A Gated Recurrent Unit processes frames one after another and keeps a running memory of 96 numbers. Each step it decides what to remember and what to forget. SONA runs one per band, so each band tracks its own recent history: "this band has hummed steadily for two seconds, so it is probably fan noise".

Sigmoid output

The last step squashes any number into the range 0 to 1, which is exactly what a mask value must be.

Chapter 16

GTCRN, put together

In one sentenceGTCRN reads the features, detects local patterns with four gated dilated convolution blocks, tracks each band over time with a GRU, and outputs a mask value per band per frame.

GTCRN stands for Gated Temporal Convolutional Recurrent Network: gated (the switches), temporal convolutional (the dilated filters over time), recurrent (the GRU memory). It is based on a published design from ICASSP 2024 that targets very low computing cost.

  1. Stem. A 1×3 convolution turns the 3 features per band into 96 learned channels per band.
  2. Four gated blocks. Each applies a 3×3 dilated convolution (dilations 1, 2, 4, 8), the gate, normalisation and the residual add.
  3. Band GRU. For each of the 32 bands, a GRU with 96 memory units reads the frames in order.
  4. Head. A final linear layer and sigmoid give one mask value per band per frame.

The exact configuration, written in the project as ch96 · h96 · 4 blocks, means 96 channels, 96 memory units, 4 blocks. In total: 722,209 parameters.

Chapter 17

The loss: what "wrong" means during training

In one sentenceSONA's training score combines three views of the error: is the waveform right, is the spectrogram right, and is it right at several levels of detail?

The loss decides what the network cares about, so it is one of the most important choices. SONA's is:

loss = − SI-SDR + 1.25 × magnitude loss + 0.25 × multi-resolution magnitude loss

− SI-SDR

SI-SDR measures how close the output waveform is to the clean one, in decibels, ignoring overall volume (Chapter 19 explains it fully). Higher SI-SDR is better, so the loss uses its negative: minimising the loss maximises SI-SDR.

Magnitude loss (weight 1.25)

Compares the output spectrogram with the clean spectrogram, band by band, on a log scale that matches hearing. It keeps the tone of the voice right.

Multi-resolution loss (weight 0.25)

The same comparison at three slice sizes: 256, 512 and 1,024 samples. Short slices catch timing errors, long slices catch pitch errors, so artefacts that one size misses get caught by another.

The weights 1.25 and 0.25 were chosen by experiment: the first sweep picked the model size, then the "loss-focus" runs tried different mixes, and this one scored best. Adding the multi-resolution term was the final improvement before the model was locked.

Chapter 18

The data, and how the final model was chosen

In one sentenceSONA learned from VoiceBank-DEMAND, was tested on unseen speakers and noises plus a completely different dataset, and its exact design was picked from a 16-way comparison.

DatasetUsed forSizeWhat is special
VoiceBank-DEMAND (train)Training2,000 pairsStudio speech mixed with real recorded noise (DEMAND) at known levels; the clean version of every clip exists
VoiceBank-DEMAND (test)Main test824 clipsTwo speakers and noise types never used in training; the standard benchmark in this research area
MS-SNSD (test)External test1,100 clipsMicrosoft's separate collection: different speakers, microphones and noises (air conditioner, babble, typing, vacuum, doors…) at −5 to +10 dB

Choosing the design

  1. Pilot. A first GTCRN run confirmed the idea worked.
  2. Sweep. 16 combinations were trained: 64 or 96 channels, 96 or 128 memory units, 4 or 5 blocks, two loss weights. The best was 96 / 96 / 4.
  3. Loss focus. That design was retrained with different loss mixes; adding the multi-resolution term won.
  4. Challengers. Three heavier variants (Mamba, governed, residual) were trained to see if more capacity helps. None beat the plain model (Chapter 26).
  5. Locked. The winner was frozen. Every result in this guide uses that frozen model.
Part E

Measuring quality

"It sounds better" is not evidence. These chapters explain every score the project reports and how to read it.

Chapter 19

Every score, explained

In one sentenceMost scores compare the cleaned speech against the original clean recording; each one looks at a different aspect, so the project always reports several.

SNR and SI-SDR: how close is the waveform?

SI-SDR (scale-invariant signal-to-distortion ratio) asks: if we line up the cleaned output with the true clean speech, how much of the output is the speech and how much is leftover error? It is a signal-to-noise ratio where "noise" means every kind of remaining error: leftover background, distortion, damaged speech.

1. scale the clean speech s to best match the output ŝ → target = α·s 2. everything else in the output is error → error = ŝ − target 3. SI-SDR = 10 × log10( power of target ÷ power of error )

"Scale-invariant" means turning the volume up or down does not change the score; only the shape of the signal counts. Plain SNR is the same idea without that volume adjustment.

The most important version is the SI-SDR improvement (SI-SDRi): SI-SDR of the output minus SI-SDR of the original noisy input. It answers "how much closer to clean did we get?". +3 dB is a noticeable improvement, +10 dB is a large one, and a negative value means the method made things worse than doing nothing.

PESQ · about 1 to 4.5

Perceptual Evaluation of Speech Quality, an international telecom standard (ITU-T P.862). It models human hearing and predicts the quality score a panel of listeners would give. Around 1 is very poor, above 3 is good. Noisy VoiceBank input scores 1.97.

STOI · 0 to 1

Short-Time Objective Intelligibility predicts how much of the speech a listener could understand, by comparing the rhythm of energy in speech bands over short windows. 0.92 means about 92% intelligible. It cares about understanding, not pleasantness.

ESTOI · 0 to 1

Extended STOI, a stricter version that also checks how bands move together. It is more sensitive to changes in intelligibility in difficult noise.

LSD · dB, lower is better

Log-Spectral Distance: the average difference between the output's spectrogram and the clean spectrogram, in decibels. It measures how faithfully the tone and texture are restored.

RTF · lower is faster

Real-Time Factor = processing time ÷ audio length. RTF 0.1 means 10 seconds of audio take 1 second to process (10× faster than real time). Anything below 1 can keep up with live audio.

WER · lower is better

Word Error Rate: the share of words a speech recogniser gets wrong. Used in Chapter 27 to check whether cleaning helps machines as well as people.

Why it matters for SONA: the scores can disagree. A method can win on SI-SDR and lose on PESQ (Chapter 25), or improve quality without improving intelligibility (Chapter 24). That is why no single number is ever presented alone.
Chapter 20

The original baseline: always compare with doing nothing

In one sentenceEvery result is shown next to the score of the original, unprocessed audio, because a method is only useful if it beats leaving the audio alone.

A score on its own can mislead. Suppose a method reaches intelligibility 0.80. Is that good? If the noisy input was 0.70, yes. If the noisy input was already 0.82, the method made things worse. So SONA always shows the original (no processing) score as the reference point.

  • For improvement scores like SI-SDRi, the original is 0 by definition: the input compared with itself has improved by nothing.
  • For absolute scores like PESQ, STOI and LSD, the original has its own value, and each method should beat it.

On VoiceBank, the original audio scores: PESQ 1.97, STOI 0.921, ESTOI 0.787, LSD 10.50 dB. These come from the project's frozen benchmark and match the conference paper.

Why it matters for SONA: adding this baseline everywhere exposed two honest findings that are easy to miss otherwise: on unfamiliar audio, intelligibility stays at the original level (Chapter 24), and block-by-block streaming lowers intelligibility below the original (Chapter 30).
Chapter 21

Statistics: is a difference real?

In one sentenceBecause scores vary from clip to clip, the project uses statistical tests to check that a difference between two methods is consistent and not luck.

If method A beats method B by 0.1 dB on average over 824 clips, is A really better? Maybe A won on a few easy clips by chance. Two tools answer this:

Wilcoxon signed-rank test

Looks at the clip-by-clip differences (A minus B on the same clip) and asks whether positive differences outweigh negative ones more than chance would explain. It gives a p-value: the probability of seeing a difference this consistent if the methods were really equal. Below 0.05 is the usual bar; SONA's main results reach p < 0.000001.

Bootstrap confidence interval

Re-samples the 824 clips with replacement 10,000 times, recomputes the average difference each time, and reports the range where 95% of those averages fall. If the range does not include zero, the difference is reliable.

Everyday comparison: a coin that lands heads 6 times in 10 might be fair. One that lands heads 600 times in 1,000 almost certainly is not. Statistics measures how surprising a result is given how many tries you had.

One caution the project takes seriously: with 824 clips, even tiny differences become "statistically significant". Significant does not mean audible. A difference of 0.016 PESQ can be real and still too small for anyone to hear.

How to read this table, row by row

  • Original: the starting point. Intelligibility is already 0.921, because VoiceBank noise is moderate; quality (PESQ 1.97) is poor.
  • GTCRN: 9.93 dB closer to clean, quality up from 1.97 to 2.52, intelligibility up slightly (0.921 → 0.930), spectral error almost halved (10.50 → 6.47). Better on every score than the original.
  • Transformer: slightly better intelligibility and spectral distance than GTCRN, but 0.85 dB less SI-SDR improvement. No model wins every column, which is why several scores are shown.
  • Classical methods: all have negative SI-SDR improvement and lower intelligibility than the original. They remove some noise but damage the speech more than they help. This held in all 5 noise types and all 4 noise levels tested, with no exceptions.
Why it matters for SONA: this is the central result of the conference paper: on realistic noise, fixed rules are worse than doing nothing, and a small learned model is a large improvement.
Chapter 24

Unfamiliar audio: the MS-SNSD test

In one sentenceOn a completely different dataset, SONA still makes speech cleaner, but it no longer makes it easier to understand.

A model can do well on a test set simply because it resembles the training data, even with unseen speakers. The real test of whether it learned "speech in general" is a dataset from somewhere else entirely. MS-SNSD has different speakers, different microphones, different noises and harder noise levels (down to −5 dB).

ModelSI-SDR gainPESQSTOIESTOI
Original (no processing)0.00—0.8180.668
GTCRN+3.151.400.8160.690
Causal Transformer+2.591.320.8040.664
  • Quality still improves, but much less: +3.15 dB here against +9.93 dB on VoiceBank.
  • Intelligibility does not improve. STOI is 0.818 before and 0.816 after GTCRN, essentially unchanged. The Transformer lowers it to 0.804. Only the stricter ESTOI rises slightly for GTCRN (0.668 → 0.690).
  • GTCRN generalises better than the Transformer on every score.

Plainly: on recordings unlike its training data, SONA removes noise but does not yet make words easier to follow. The clearest fix is training on more varied data: more speakers, microphones, rooms and noise types.

The MS-SNSD original scores were computed over all 1,100 clips with the project's own metric code; PESQ was not available for that run.

Chapter 25

Magnitude mask or complex mask?

In one sentenceA variant that also corrects phase got a better waveform score but a slightly worse perceptual score: a trade-off, not a free upgrade.

Chapter 9 explained that the main model keeps the noisy phase. A complex mask instead predicts two numbers per band (a real and an imaginary part), which together change both strength and timing. To test it fairly, both versions were trained identically on 5,000 clips and tested on the same 824 clips.

ScoreMagnitude maskComplex maskDifferencep-value
SI-SDR gain (dB)9.7310.04+0.31< 0.000001
STOI0.9290.931+0.002< 0.000001
PESQ2.4942.478−0.0160.005

The waveform and intelligibility scores improve reliably, but PESQ drops slightly, and that drop is also reliable. If the project had only measured SI-SDR, it would have reported a clear win that is not the whole story. Both versions are available in the app.

Chapter 26

Experiments that taught us something

In one sentenceSeveral ideas were tested properly and did not help; reporting them is part of doing the research honestly.

1 · Adapting on the fly (the original idea)

The project started with an ambitious plan: let the model fine-tune itself on every new clip after deployment, with no clean reference, by maximising a quality estimate from a separate model (TorchAudio-SQUIM). This is called test-time adaptation. Results: without safeguards, it hurt (MS-SNSD PESQ 1.323 → 1.307), because the model learned to please the quality estimator rather than to clean the speech. With a strict safety guard that rejects any change that moves the output too far, it never hurt, but the gain was essentially zero (SI-SDR gain 9.082 → 9.079 dB). The app keeps it as an experimental switch that reports whether the guard accepted the change.

2 · Bigger models did not help

VariantIdeaSI-SDR gain
GTCRN (plain)the locked model+9.93
Governed GTCRNpredicts a cautious and an aggressive mask and learns how to blend them+9.89
Residual GTCRNadds a small correction step after the GRU+9.87
Mamba-GTCRNadds a modern "state-space" memory layer for longer context+9.84

Extra complexity added cost without adding quality, so the simplest model was kept.

Chapter 27

Making the model smaller, and the effect on speech recognition

In one sentenceAlmost all the quality lost when shrinking the model came from one tiny layer, and audio cleaned for human ears turned out to be slightly worse for machines.

Quantisation: storing weights in fewer bits

Each weight is normally stored as a 32-bit decimal number. Quantisation stores it as an 8-bit integer instead (INT8), which makes the file about a third of the size: 2.84 MB → 0.95 MB. The cost is rounding error, like rounding every price to the nearest rupee.

Measuring the damage layer by layer revealed something striking: the first layer (the stem) holds only 0.133% of the weights but caused 98.7% of the quality loss. Keeping just that layer at full precision ("stem-exempt") gave SI-SDR 18.375 dB against 18.377 dB for the full-precision model, a difference too small to measure reliably. It was also smaller and faster than quantising everything. On the processors tested, INT8 ran about 1.4 times slower than full precision, so the benefit is size, not speed.

Speech recognition (word error rate)

The project fed cleaned and uncleaned audio to Whisper, a well-known speech recogniser. On VoiceBank, its word error rate rose from 3.45% to 4.28% on cleaned audio, a 24% relative increase, confirmed with a second recogniser (+23%) and on MS-SNSD (+47%). Enhancement tuned for human listeners can remove subtle cues a recogniser relies on. The practical lesson: give a recogniser the original audio and give people the cleaned version.

Part G

The system

The model is one part. Around it sits a controller that shapes the sound, an application for using it, and a real-time engine.

Chapter 28

The controller: scenes, modes and sound shaping

In one sentenceA tiny classifier recognises the kind of environment, picks a sound mode, and that mode sets how strongly to denoise and how to shape the final sound.

Scene classifier

A very small network (1,716 parameters) labels the audio as speech, music, traffic, fan, crowd, mixed or unknown. On recordings from speakers and sessions it never saw, it is right about 75% of the time (0.748).

Modes

Speech, strong speech, podcast, hearing, music, gaming and studio. Each mode is a preset of the settings below. "Automatic" picks a mode from the scene.

Noise removal strength

Blends the original and the cleaned audio: 1.00 means "trust the model fully". Testing showed going above 1 over-corrects and lowers quality.

Equaliser (EQ)

Boosts or cuts 8 frequency ranges from 31 Hz to 4 kHz, like the bass and treble controls on a stereo, to make speech clearer or fuller.

Compressor

Turns loud moments down and evens out the level, so quiet words are not lost and sudden peaks do not startle.

Limiter and hum filter

The limiter stops the output from ever exceeding the maximum level (no distortion). The hum filter removes electrical mains hum at 50 or 60 Hz and its multiples.

Scene memory lets a user save their preferred settings for a scene ("in traffic, use hearing mode"), which are then applied automatically.

Chapter 29

The application

In one sentenceA web application that runs on your own computer and puts every part of the project, from the models to the benchmarks, behind simple pages.

Enhance

Pick one of ten real test clips (each with its clean reference) or upload a file, then press Enhance. Settings are optional, in a side panel.

Results

Switch between original, cleaned, removed noise and clean reference while playing; see before/after spectrograms, a live visualiser and four headline numbers, each shown as original → cleaned.

Compare

Real-time

Simulates live processing in small blocks and shows the delay, speed and quality cost.

About

Private

Chapter 30

Running in real time

In one sentenceA live device must process audio in small blocks as it arrives, finish each block before the next one is due, and the block size trades delay against quality.

Processing a saved file is easy: the model can look at the entire recording. A live device, such as a headset, cannot see the future; it receives sound continuously. So it works in blocks:

  1. Wait until one block of audio has arrived (for example 128 ms).
  2. Clean that block with the model.
  3. Fade the edges and overlap-add it with the previous block so there are no clicks at the joins.
  4. Send it to the speaker, then repeat for the next block.
  • Latency (delay): you cannot output a block before you have heard it, so the delay is at least one block. Bigger blocks mean longer delay.
  • Deadline: each block must be processed in less time than it takes for the next to arrive. Missing it causes a glitch.
  • Speed: SONA processes audio about 10 times faster than real time on a single laptop processor core (RTF 0.08 to 0.10), and over 100 times faster on a graphics card. Speed is not the problem.

The catch: the current streaming engine cleans each block independently, so the model forgets everything at every block boundary. Bigger blocks help, but even at 256 ms the gain (+6.5 dB) is well below whole-file processing (+9.2 dB). Intelligibility shows the same thing more sharply: on this clip at 128 ms blocks, STOI falls to 0.693, which is below the original's 0.771, while whole-file processing raises it to 0.800. Fixing this, by carrying the model's memory from one 8 ms frame to the next, is the first engineering task of Phase 2.

Part H

Phase 2: the hardware device

Phase 1 proved the method works on audio files. Phase 2 makes it work live, on a small device you can wear or carry.

What Phase 2 builds

PartWhat it doesWhy it is needed

Chapter 32

Phase 2 plan and targets

In one sentenceFive milestones take the project from wiring the board to measuring a working device against clear targets.

  1. H1 · Bring-up. Connect board, audio codec, microphone and headphones; measure the delay of the audio path alone before any model runs.
  2. H2 · Model on the board. Convert GTCRN to a portable format (ONNX), measure speed on the board's processor, and use the stem-exempt 8-bit version from Chapter 27 to save memory.
  3. H3 · True frame-by-frame streaming. Carry the model's memory between 8 ms frames and replace the clip-wide normalisation with a per-frame one, then fine-tune. Goal: live quality equal to whole-file quality, removing the loss shown in Chapter 30.
  4. H4 · Device and controls. A continuous audio loop (capture → model → playback) that never stalls, the controller running on the board, a physical mode button, and the web interface reachable from a phone over Wi-Fi.
  5. H5 · Evaluation. Measure delay, processor load, temperature, battery life and dropouts over long runs; record real rooms; run a listening test with volunteers.
TargetValueReason
Microphone-to-ear delay< 50 msone 32 ms window plus buffering; longer delays are distracting while talking
Real-time factor on the board< 0.5leaves half the time budget for the controller and the operating system
Dropouts0 in 30 minutesa single glitch is audible
Live quality≈ whole-file qualityPhase 1 whole-file result: +9.9 dB SI-SDR gain on VoiceBank
Battery life≥ 3 hoursa practical session length

Phase 2 values are design targets, to be confirmed by measurement on the real hardware.

Chapter 33

Glossary

Amplitude
How big a sound wave's pressure swings are; heard as loudness.
Baseline (original)
The score of the unprocessed noisy audio; every method should beat it.
Bark scale
Frequency bands spaced like human hearing: narrow at low pitch, wide at high pitch. SONA uses 32.
Batch
A group of training examples processed together before one weight update. SONA uses 8.
Causal
Uses only past and present input, never the future. Required for live use.
Classical / DSP
Noise reduction by fixed formulas rather than learning.
Convolution
A small grid of weights that slides across the input to detect a pattern.
dB (decibel)
A logarithmic ratio scale; +10 dB means 10 times the power.
Dilation
Spacing out a convolution's taps so it sees further back in time.
Epoch
One full pass through all the training data. SONA trained for 50.
FFT
Fast Fourier Transform: the algorithm that finds a sound's frequency ingredients.
Frame / hop
A 32 ms slice of audio; the hop is the 8 ms step between slices.
Frequency
How many times per second a wave repeats, in hertz (Hz); heard as pitch.
GRU
Gated Recurrent Unit: a layer with memory that reads a sequence one step at a time.
GTCRN
Gated Temporal Convolutional Recurrent Network: SONA's 722k-parameter model.
Inference
Using a trained model on new audio (as opposed to training it).
Latency
The delay between sound going in and cleaned sound coming out.
Loss
The number training tries to minimise; measures how wrong the output is.
LSD
Log-spectral distance: average spectrogram difference in dB; lower is better.
Magnitude / phase
The strength and the timing offset of each frequency in a frame.
Mask
A value from 0 to 1 per band per frame saying how much to keep.
Nyquist limit
The highest frequency a sample rate can capture: half the rate (8 kHz at 16 kHz).
ONNX
A portable model format that runs on many kinds of processor.
Overfitting
Memorising training examples instead of learning the general pattern.
Overlap-add
Joining overlapping processed slices back into continuous sound without seams.
Parameter / weight
One adjustable number inside a network.
PESQ
Perceptual quality score (ITU-T P.862), about 1 to 4.5.
p-value
How likely a difference this consistent would be if the methods were truly equal.
Quantisation
Storing weights with fewer bits (e.g. 8 instead of 32) to shrink the model.
RTF
Real-time factor: processing time ÷ audio length; below 1 keeps up with live audio.
SONA
Self-supervised Online Neural Audio engine, the project's name (Chapter 1).
Sample rate
Measurements per second. SONA uses 16,000.
SI-SDR(i)
How close the output waveform is to clean speech, in dB (and its improvement over the original).
SNR
Signal-to-noise ratio: how much stronger the voice is than the noise, in dB.
Spectrogram
A picture of sound: time across, frequency up, loudness as brightness.
STFT
Short-Time Fourier Transform: the slicing-and-FFT process that makes a spectrogram.
STOI / ESTOI
Predicted intelligibility, 0 to 1 (ESTOI is the stricter version).
Test set
Data held back and used only for final scoring, never for training.
WER
Word error rate of a speech recogniser; lower is better.
SONA · final-year project · Phase 1 software complete, Phase 2 hardware in planning. Results come from the project's frozen benchmark runs; the original MS-SNSD scores were computed over the full test set with the project's metric code. Audio samples are from the public MS-SNSD test set.
